section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Vectors as Arrows
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as directed segments in 2D space. Visualize them as movements: v = [2, 1] is 'go right 2, up 1'. Establish that scaling (c*v) and addition (v+w) form the building blocks of all operations.
section_1.example: A delivery drone moving along vector A (North) and vector B (East).

section_2.title: Linear Combinations and Span
section_2.content: Define a linear combination as 'c1v1 + c2v2'. Introduce 'Span' as the set of all possible reach points. Use a grid animation: show the drone moving in varying steps of A and B, gradually filling the entire 2D plane.
section_2.example: Two vectors A=[1,0] and B=[0,1] act as building blocks; by combining them, the drone can reach any point (x, y) on the map.

section_3.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Vector
section_3.content: Explain linear dependence visually: if vector C lies on the same line as A and B, it adds no 'new' dimensions. It is redundant. Use an animation showing a third vector being 'squashed' into the existing line.
section_3.example: Three robots walking: Robot C follows the exact path of Robot A. If Robot A is already there, Robot C provides no new navigation capability.

section_4.title: The Concept of Basis
section_4.content: Define a Basis as the 'minimal set' of vectors that span the space without redundancy (linearly independent). Emphasize that a basis is the most efficient 'coordinate system' for a space.
section_4.example: To describe a room, you need exactly 3 dimensions (Length, Width, Height). If you add a 4th measurement that is just a sum of the others, it's not a basis—it's redundant information.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Wrap up by linking the concepts: Vectors build Combinations -> Combinations create a Span -> Removing redundant vectors leaves us with a Basis. Connect back to the drone navigation example.
section_5.example: A GPS system uses a basis of 3 satellites to pinpoint any position in 3D space. Adding a 4th satellite makes the system more robust but technically redundant for the base span.

section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Vectors as Arrows
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as directed segments in 2D space. Visualize them as movements: v = [2, 1] is 'go right 2, up 1'. Establish that scaling (c*v) and addition (v+w) form the building blocks of all operations.
section_1.example: A delivery drone moving along vector A (North) and vector B (East).

section_2.title: Linear Combinations and Span
section_2.content: Define a linear combination as 'c1v1 + c2v2'. Introduce 'Span' as the set of all possible reach points. Use a grid animation: show the drone moving in varying steps of A and B, gradually filling the entire 2D plane.
section_2.example: Two vectors A=[1,0] and B=[0,1] act as building blocks; by combining them, the drone can reach any point (x, y) on the map.

section_3.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Vector
section_3.content: Explain linear dependence visually: if vector C lies on the same line as A and B, it adds no 'new' dimensions. It is redundant. Use an animation showing a third vector being 'squashed' into the existing line.
section_3.example: Three robots walking: Robot C follows the exact path of Robot A. If Robot A is already there, Robot C provides no new navigation capability.

section_4.title: The Concept of Basis
section_4.content: Define a Basis as the 'minimal set' of vectors that span the space without redundancy (linearly independent). Emphasize that a basis is the most efficient 'coordinate system' for a space.
section_4.example: To describe a room, you need exactly 3 dimensions (Length, Width, Height). If you add a 4th measurement that is just a sum of the others, it's not a basis—it's redundant information.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Wrap up by linking the concepts: Vectors build Combinations -> Combinations create a Span -> Removing redundant vectors leaves us with a Basis. Connect back to the drone navigation example.
section_5.example: A GPS system uses a basis of 3 satellites to pinpoint any position in 3D space. Adding a 4th satellite makes the system more robust but technically redundant for the base span.
